-88.12060,41.56280.name: Kindbody-Crest Hill
-88.12060,41.56280.desc: A fertility clinic reporting to the CDC's National ART Surveillance System. Medical director: Angie Beltsos, MD. A fertility clinic is where human embryos are made, selected and stored, and where assisted reproduction happens, like IVF, ICSI, egg and sperm donation, freezing embryos and eggs for later. Reporting is required of every US clinic performing assisted reproduction, under the Fertility Clinic Success Rate and Certification Act, so this is close to a complete register rather than a list of members. What it records is cycles started, which is not the same as children born.

76.96687,8.49239.desc: A BSL3+ laboratory, operational. Run by Ministry of Science & Technology (Department of Biotechnology). It is categorised as a public health laboratory, working on human health. Operational or announced: 2022. It stands in a built-up area, with more than fifty thousand people living within two and a half miles. There is no international register of laboratories at this containment level and no obligation to declare one, so this record comes from a research project rather than a regulator. What that project could not find out is absent here too.

-87.62500,41.88800.name: ARCH Venture Partners
-87.62500,41.88800.desc: One of the most influential early-stage investors in biotechnology, founding and funding companies across this map from Illumina onward. Venture money sets the clock: a fund must return capital within a fixed period, which rewards moving fast and getting big long before any regulator sees a product. That deadline shapes what gets built more than any scientific judgement does.

-76.14740,43.04810.name: American Chestnut Foundation — Darling 58
-76.14740,43.04810.desc: The engineered blight-tolerant chestnut was studied for about seven years before anyone noticed the tree in the trials was not the tree in the application — two lines had been mixed up, and the one actually tested carries a second gene broken by the insertion, resists blight only patchily, and dies at high rates. The Foundation withdrew its support in 2023. An inserted gene lands somewhere, and what it lands in the middle of is not chosen, which is why this went unnoticed for seven years by people with every reason to look. The withdrawal was announced on 8 December 2023, covering the pending petitions that would have authorised distribution outside permitted research plots — four months after the Foundation was still promoting the tree for restoration. Its published reasoning is the rarest document in this facet: the mislabelling concealed changes to coding regions of the genome whose effects on growth and survival were unknown and untested, and factual errors in a petition can call into question the accuracy of everything else the applicant supplied.

-76.14740,43.04810.name: American Chestnut Research and Restoration Project — SUNY ESF
-76.14740,43.04810.desc: Developed the blight-resistant Darling 58 chestnut, carrying a wheat gene that detoxifies the fungus which killed four billion American chestnuts in the twentieth century. It is the first engineered organism proposed for release into wild forests purely to restore a species rather than to produce anything, and it has spent years in a USDA petition that the project's own supporters criticised after data problems emerged. The case is where conservation and biosafety argue directly, with no commercial interest between them. The petition filed with USDA APHIS in late 2019 sought nonregulated status — which would mean no permit, no boundary and no recall for a long-lived organism in wild woodland. In Darling 54, the line actually used in the field trials, the inserted gene sits on a different chromosome from Darling 58, the line the petitions named. The project is continuing on the Darling 54 trials and seeking adoption of that line instead, with a corrected petition.

-78.89900,35.99400.name: Precision BioSciences
-78.89900,35.99400.state: Durham, North Carolina — 302 East Pettigrew Street
-78.89900,35.99400.desc: Uses ARCUS meganucleases, a third editing chemistry distinct from both zinc fingers and CRISPR, in gene therapy and in engineered crops. Its existence matters to the carve-out argument: rules written around one molecular tool do not obviously cover organisms made with another.
